opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to the fact that the world has two very different kinds of information, and right now we don't have a single representation that handles both of them really well.

Language is discrete. It's tokens, it's symbols, and it has been compressed by humans over thousands of years. Every word carries a lot of meaning, so a transformer predicting the next token is a very efficient way to learn reasoning, planning, common-sense knowledge, all of that. The physical world is different. Video, motion, the forces when a robot grasps something, these are continuous signals. They're high-dimensional and redundant, and a lot of the information is in fine details: how light reflects, how an object deforms, how things move frame to frame. If you force that into discrete tokens too aggressively, you lose fidelity. And for physical AI, fidelity matters. A robot can't act on a blurry understanding of where the cup is.

So at this stage, a two-tower design lets each side do what it's good at. The discrete side, the language-model-like part, carries the reasoning and the high-level understanding: what is happening, what should happen next, what the task is. The continuous side, which is more diffusion-based, carries the rich physical detail and generates or predicts the world at high quality. Then you connect them so they can talk to each other, with the reasoning conditioning the generation and the perception grounding the reasoning.

Is this the final answer? I don't think so. In the long run, I'd love to see one unified model that handles both natively, and many people, including us, are exploring that. But research is also about being practical. Today the best language models and the best visual generative models come from fairly different recipes, and each has been optimized very heavily. If you try to merge them too early, you often get something worse at both. With two towers we can take advantage of the progress on both sides right now and build something useful for robotics and autonomous driving developers, while we keep learning what a truly unified world model should look like.

So I'd call it the right engineering choice for now, rather than a philosophical claim about the end state.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think of it less as a philosophical commitment and more as being pragmatic about where the technology is right now.

When we started Cosmos, the goal was clear: we want a world foundation model that can simulate the physical world, so that robots and autonomous vehicles can be trained and tested in simulation rather than only in the real world. To do that well, the model has to understand two very different things. One is the fine-grained, continuous nature of the physical world — how light falls on a surface, how a cup tips over, how a car's suspension responds on a bumpy road. The other is more semantic, more abstract — what objects are, what actions mean, how to follow an instruction like "pick up the red block and put it in the bin."

Those two kinds of information really want different representations. Continuous tokens, with a diffusion-based approach, are very good at capturing visual fidelity and physical detail. You get smooth, high-quality video that respects physics. Discrete tokens, with an autoregressive approach, inherit a lot from what's worked so well in language models — they're efficient, they compose well with text and actions, and they're easier to plug into a reasoning or planning loop.

If you try to force everything into one representation today, you tend to compromise somewhere. Pure autoregressive on discrete video tokens loses visual quality and has to deal with very long sequences. Pure diffusion is great at generation but harder to use as a controllable, step-by-step planner that talks to a language model.

So we said, let's build both. Let's have a diffusion tower and an autoregressive tower, share the data pipeline, share the tokenizers where it makes sense, and let developers pick the one that fits their problem. A robotics team doing policy learning might want the discrete path. A team generating training data for perception might want the highest-fidelity continuous path.

The other reason is that this is a very fast-moving field. I don't think anyone can say with confidence which paradigm wins in two years. Keeping both alive lets us learn from both, and frankly, the two towers are already borrowing ideas from each other. My expectation is that over time they converge — that we'll have a more unified architecture — but I'd rather arrive at that convergence through evidence than by guessing early and locking ourselves in.

So "two-tower" is really a statement about this stage. It's the honest answer to the question of what works today, while leaving the door open for where things are going.

astra-6.text:
I think of it as giving us two complementary ways to represent the world. A discrete representation is useful when you want to model a sequence of tokens and use the machinery of autoregressive prediction. A continuous representation is useful when you want to preserve fine visual detail and model smooth changes in a scene.

For Cosmos, we want to explore both capabilities without forcing one representation to do everything. If you commit entirely to discrete tokens, you have to manage the information lost through quantization. If you commit entirely to continuous representations, you give up some of the convenience of working with token sequences.

So at this stage, the two-tower approach is a practical choice. It lets us develop each path around its strengths and learn where each is most useful. I wouldn’t say it has to be the final architecture. The important thing is to build a foundation that gives us room to improve prediction, visual fidelity, and efficiency as we learn.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that discrete and continuous representations have different strengths. A discrete representation gives you a sequence of tokens, which fits naturally with autoregressive modeling. You can use that structure to reason about what happens next. A continuous representation is well suited to generation where you want to preserve subtle details and produce smooth motion.

For Cosmos, we want to explore both capabilities. If we commit to a single representation too early, we may introduce a bottleneck for one of them. A two-tower architecture lets us develop each representation for the task it serves best, while exploring how information can move between them.

So I would view it as a practical choice at this stage. We want to learn where discrete modeling helps, where continuous modeling helps, and how to combine their strengths.
